Your bathroom walls deserve just as much attention as any other room in your home — yet wall art is often the last thing people think to add. Whether you have a compact cloakroom or a generous family bathroom, the right artwork can shift the whole feel of the space from purely functional to something genuinely considered. This guide walks you through practical bathroom art ideas: how to choose the right size, theme, and framing, and where to hang pieces for maximum impact.

Bathroom art ideas work best in small spaces when you choose moisture-resistant framing, scale artwork to no more than two-thirds the wall width, and focus on one or two well-placed pieces rather than filling every surface — the result is a bathroom that feels intentional, polished, and genuinely personal. 

Quick Answer: The best bathroom art ideas focus on three things: choosing moisture-resistant framing (metal or acrylic rather than wood), scaling artwork to no more than two-thirds of the wall width, and picking calm, nature-inspired or abstract themes that suit the relaxed mood of the space. One well-placed anchor piece — above the toilet or at eye level on the main wall — creates more impact than several smaller items. Stick to one or two carefully chosen prints and the room will feel intentional and polished.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Key Takeaways:

  • Bathroom art ideas are most effective when artwork is scaled correctly — aim for pieces no more than two-thirds the width of the wall if hanging solo, and always measure before buying.
  • Moisture-resistant framing is essential in bathrooms — metal or acrylic frames outperform wood in humid environments, and canvas-wrapped prints are the most durable option for long-term use.
  • Nature-inspired themes, abstract prints in muted tones, and monochrome photography are the most versatile wall art choices for bathrooms as they complement a wide range of colour schemes and create a calm, restful atmosphere.
  • The wall above the toilet is the most underused placement opportunity in a small bathroom — a single medium-sized framed print here immediately makes the space feel more considered and complete.
  • One anchor piece at eye level creates more impact in a small bathroom than multiple smaller items competing for attention — simplicity is the most effective styling principle in compact spaces.

When it comes to decorating a small bathroom, bathroom art ideas might not be the first thing that comes to mind. After all, compact spaces can feel limiting in terms of style. But adding elegant framed art can completely transform your bathroom, making it feel more intentional, cosy, and effortlessly chic.

In this guide, I'll share step-by-step strategies, creative ideas, and insider tips to help you incorporate sophisticated framed art into your small bathroom. Whether you want to create a spa-like feel, inject some personality, or simply tie together a design scheme, this blog has you covered.

Why Framed Art Belongs in Small Bathrooms

Bathrooms, especially small ones, are too often overlooked when decorating — yet they're one of the most used spaces in our homes. Adding framed art to your bathroom brings personality, warmth, and a sense of intention that makes the space feel genuinely designed rather than just functional.

  • Adds a touch of luxury: Framed artwork instantly elevates your bathroom, making it feel polished and finished.
  • Injects personality: Whether you love minimalist designs, bold colours, vintage photography, or nature-inspired art, choosing artwork that resonates with you makes your bathroom feel like an extension of your personal style.
  • Creates focal points: In a small space, strategic artwork draws focus to specific areas, making the room feel more structured.
  • Sets a calming mood: A serene botanical print or soft abstract piece creates the kind of calm, restful atmosphere that makes a bathroom feel genuinely pleasant to spend time in.

How to Choose the Right Art for Small Bathrooms

Choosing the perfect art pieces requires balancing style, size, and practicality. Here's how to approach it:

Dimensions Matter

In a small bathroom, proportions are everything. Oversized art pieces can dominate the room, whilst pieces that are too small may feel insignificant. Measure your wall spaces before selecting artwork — aim for pieces that are no more than two-thirds the width of the wall if hanging solo. The colour of your bathroom vanity also sets the overall tone, so choose artwork that complements rather than competes with it.

Themes That Work

Bathrooms are naturally calm spaces, so lean into themes like:

  • Nature-inspired art: Landscapes, florals, or botanicals.
  • Abstract pieces: Soft geometric patterns or muted tones add a modern twist.
  • Photography: Monochrome prints of architecture or cityscapes are a classic choice.
  • A touch of humour: A small, witty quote or quirky image can add charm to a small bathroom.

If you want a set that does all the work for you, these bathroom wall pictures in monochrome botanical illustrations are a brilliant ready-made option.

SHOP HERE

 

For those who love travel, incorporating artwork from your favourite destinations adds a genuinely personal touch — a framed postcard or map print works beautifully in a small bathroom.

If you want a set that does all the work for you, these pictures for bathroom walls in rich botanical greens are one of our most popular farmhouse-style choices.

Colour Schemes

Follow the existing colours in your bathroom to ensure the art complements the overall look. If your bathroom has neutral tones, consider bold or metallic accents in your artwork. For bathrooms with vibrant tiles or walls, soft and understated tones in the art will balance the space without adding visual noise.

Creative Placement Bathroom Art Ideas for Your Wall

Placement can make or break how your artwork makes an impact. Here are the most effective spots for small bathroom art:

  • Above the toilet: An often overlooked wall, this is a great spot for a small to medium-sized framed print.
  • Above the towel rack: Adds dimension and prevents the wall from looking bare.
  • On a floating shelf: Place a small framed print on a shelf alongside candles and greenery for a layered look.
  • In front of the mirror: If you have a mirror with reflective wall space behind it, hang art here to double its visual impact.
  • Back of the door: A frequently overlooked area that works well for lightweight prints or small framed pieces.

If you want a set that handles the hard work for you, these bathroom pictures for wall in a Shabby Chic floral set of three are a brilliant starting point for a soft, vintage-inspired scheme.

Best Framing Options for Humid Spaces

Bathrooms are humid environments, so protecting your art is essential. Here's how to frame intelligently:

  • Frame materials: Opt for moisture-resistant materials such as metal or acrylic over wood, which can warp over time.
  • Glass covers: Ensure your framed art has a glass or acrylic sheet cover to shield it from moisture.
  • Canvas-wrapped art: An excellent choice for humid environments due to its durability and resilience. Unlike traditional framed art, canvas-wrapped pieces are tightly stretched over a sturdy frame, reducing the risk of sagging or damage. The canvas material is impermeable, preventing moisture buildup that can lead to mildew and ensuring the artwork retains its colours and structural integrity over time.

If you want art that truly lasts in a steamy space, our dedicated guide to moisture resistant art for bathroom walls covers the materials, frames and placement rules that make the real difference.

Whether you're decorating a newborn's nursery or refreshing a teenager's bedroom, the right artwork does far more than fill an empty wall — it shapes the atmosphere, sparks imagination, and reflects a growing personality.

Struggling to choose wall art that your child won't outgrow in six months? The secret to creating a room that evolves with your child lies in understanding children's room wall art—age-appropriate artwork that balances current interests with lasting appeal. Choose flexible display systems such as picture ledges so you can swap prints easily as interests evolve. A grey and beige living room strikes the perfect balance between warmth and sophistication when styled with care. This guide walks you through shade selection, texture layering, furniture finishes, and accent colours to help you create a space that feels both inviting and beautifully considered. Whether you're starting from scratch or refreshing an existing room, you'll find practical inspiration to suit every taste.

Have you ever walked into a room that seemed calm, inviting, and sophisticated all at once—and wondered how they pulled it off? You might be surprised to learn that the secret often lies in something as simple as the colour palette. A grey and beige living room might sound like a safe choice, but with the right approach, it can become a stylish sanctuary full of personality and warmth.

Quick Answer: To style a neutral living room with grey and beige tones successfully, align the undertones of both colours so they sit harmoniously — pair warm greige walls with similarly warm beige furnishings, for example. Layer contrasting textures such as velvet, linen, wool, and natural wood to add depth and prevent the scheme from feeling flat. Introduce one or two accent colours — soft terracotta, dusty sage, or muted blush — through cushions, rugs, and wall art to give the palette personality without overpowering it.

Styling a grey and beige living room successfully means balancing subtle hues with textures, lighting, and decor that breathe life into these neutral tones. If you've been hesitant to embrace this combo because it feels potentially dull, don't worry—I'm here to provide practical tips and fresh ideas. From picking the perfect accent colours to choosing furniture finishes that elevate the space, there's a lot to explore that turns understated into unforgettable.

Wall art often provides the finishing touch, framing your room's mood and adding that splash of personal flair. Whether you prefer bold statement pieces or a curated gallery wall, the right artworks can harmonise beautifully with grey and beige, enhancing both colour and calm. If you're curious, explore some stunning options in living room decor to get inspired.

Choosing the Perfect Shades for a Grey and Beige Living Room

Getting started with your grey and beige living room means deciding the undertones of these neutrals. Grey and beige might seem simple but both have a broad spectrum, from cool blues to warm taupes. Choosing the right undertone can make a significant impact on how your room feels.

Why Undertones Matter

Imagine this: a cool grey with a hint of blue paired with a warm beige that leans towards yellow. The contrast between cool and warm can create an unexpected tension that feels a bit off. But when the undertones align—say, a warm greige (grey-beige) matched with a similarly warm-toned beige—the space feels pulled together and balanced.

Tips for Selecting Shades

  • Test Samples in Your Space: Natural lighting affects colours dramatically. Always test swatches on walls or fabrics within the actual room.
  • Blend Shades: Layer different tones of grey and beige rather than choosing one flat colour. This layering adds dimension.
  • Consider the Room's Purpose: Softer beige with warmer grey tones make spaces feel cosy – perfect for living areas focused on relaxation.

Your wall colour sets the stage, but pairing it with neutral-toned wall art creates continuity. For ideas on artwork that blends naturally within these shades, see neutral tones.

Incorporating Texture and Warmth into Grey and Beige Interiors

One common worry when styling a grey and beige living room is that these neutral colours can feel too cold or bland. Texture becomes your best ally here. It's one thing to choose the right colour but layering tactile elements truly brings warmth and personality.

Key Textures to Mix In

  • Soft Fabrics: Velvets and linens add softness, especially when used on cushions or curtains.
  • Natural Fibres: Wool throws and jute or sisal rugs offer organic warmth and subtle patterning.
  • Wood Elements: Opt for wooden furniture finishes with natural grains rather than artificial surfaces.
  • Metallic Accents: Brushed gold or copper accessories provide warmth and a modern edge.

To organise your décor elements effectively, here's a simple table showing how to combine textures with colours:

Texture Colour Tone Areas to Use Effect

Wool Beige with hints of cream Throws, rugs Creates cosy, inviting feel
Natural wood Light to mid oak Furniture pieces, frames Adds earthiness and warmth
Brushed metal Warm gold, brass Lamps, hardware Introduces subtle shine

Furniture Finishes that Complement a Grey and Beige Living Room Design

Choosing the right furniture finishes can make or break your grey and beige living room's vibe. The finish adds character, connects with the colour palette, and enhances the texture play we discussed earlier.

Popular Furniture Finishes for This Palette

  • Natural Wood: Light to medium wood tones like oak or walnut inject warmth and prevent sterile atmospheres.
  • Matte Painted Surfaces: Soft grey or off-white painted finishes create calmness and pair effortlessly with textiles.
  • Brushed or Warm Metals: Brass or bronze hardware on cupboards and lighting add subtle glamour without overwhelming softness.
  • Upholstery: Linen and cotton blends in muted beige and grey shades ensure comfort without visual noise.

A client transformed their dated living room, painting wooden furniture in muted grey and replacing dull knobs with warm brass handles. They swapped an old faux leather sofa for a beige linen couch and introduced a light oak coffee table to enhance natural elements. The result: a calm, sophisticated space with layered textures and finishes that echoed the soft neutrals of their interior design concepts inspirations.

Using Accent Colours to Bring Your Grey and Beige Living Room to Life

One of the easiest ways to avoid a bland grey and beige living room is by adding well-chosen accent colours. These pops of colour inject personality and vitality, while still respecting the calming foundation of your neutrals.

Top Accent Colours for This Scheme

  • Muted Green: Deep sage or olive offer an organic, grounded feel.
  • Blush Pink: Soft and romantic, perfect for cushions or artwork.
  • Navy Blue: Adds depth and sophistication for a bolder contrast.
  • Burnt Orange: Warm and energising—great for rugs and throws.
  • Mustard Yellow: Gives a vintage, cosy vibe without overpowering.

Adding these colours through artwork, soft furnishings, or decor items seamlessly ties into the room's mood. For inspiration, check out some of the best colour combinations in wall art that complement neutral bases.

Lighting Considerations for a Soft and Inviting Grey and Beige Living Room

Lighting is often overlooked but essential when styling a grey and beige living room. The right lighting brings out undertones, highlights textures, and changes the ambiance throughout the day.

Types of Lighting to Consider

  • Ambient Lighting: Use warm LED bulbs in ceiling fixtures or recessed lights to create overall comfort.
  • Task Lighting: Choose table or floor lamps with directional lighting for reading or hobby corners.
  • Accent Lighting: Spotlights or picture lights help showcase wall art and feature decor.

Layering these types of lighting ensures versatility and mood variation. For instance, dimmable lamps make your living room adaptable from bright and lively to calm and restful. This combination enhances the soft colours of your grey and beige living room perfectly.

Once you have your palette in place, deciding which prints to hang becomes much easier — our complete guide to art style types helps you match the right visual movement to your neutral scheme.

How do you style a grey and beige living room without looking bland?

Styling a grey and beige living room to prevent it feeling bland requires thoughtful layering, contrast, and personal touches.

Start with Depth in Neutrals

Don't just pick one grey and one beige. Instead, use a spectrum of these tones. For example:

  • A medium warm beige on your sofa
  • Cooler grey walls or feature décor
  • Various cushions in lighter and darker shades

Introduce Texture and Patterns

Textures like velvet cushions, a woven wool rug, or a linen curtain give tactility. Patterns in soft geometrics or abstract forms add subtle interest without clashing with your colour scheme.

Bring in Accent Colours and Art

Effective use of accessories like throws, cushions, and living room decor introduces variety and focal points. Go for accent colours to add vibrancy and let your wall art tell a story.

What accent colours work best in a grey and beige living room?

Certain accent colours enhance the grey and beige living room's calming vibe while adding personality.

Effective Accent Choices

  • Muted Greens: Sage or olive capture natural serenity.
  • Blush Pinks: These soft hues add warmth without overwhelming.
  • Navy Blue: Offers a grounding contrast and depth.
  • Burnt Orange and Mustard Yellow: Bring vibrant energy and retro charm.

Use accent items like cushions, vases, or small furniture pieces to try these shades first. For a curated selection of wall art in these tones, colour combinations can really help guide your choices.

Which furniture finishes complement a grey and beige living room design?

Furniture finishes should emphasise the warmth and subtlety of your grey and beige colour scheme.

Recommended Finishes

  • Natural Light to Mid-tone Woods: Oak and walnut contribute earthy warmth.
  • Soft Matte Painted Surfaces: Painted furniture in grey or off-white tones complements upholstery.
  • Brushed Metals: Brass, bronze, or copper in lighting and fittings soften the look while adding visual interest.
  • Upholstered Pieces: Linen or cotton fabric ranged in beige or light grey enhance comfort and keep the palette uniform.

How do you add warmth and texture to a grey and beige living room?

Adding warmth and texture to a grey and beige living room revolves around mixing natural materials, layers, and lighting.

Effective Techniques

  • Layered Rugs and Throws: Combine woven wool rugs with soft throws to add tactile comfort.
  • Textured Cushions and Upholstery: Velvet and linen add visual and physical depth.
  • Wood and Metal Accessories: Use furniture with natural grain and warm metals for warmth.
  • Soft Lighting: Create inviting glow with warm-toned bulbs and layered fixtures.

These approaches encourage a lived-in look that feels welcoming yet refined.

Hopefully, you now have a clearer sense of how to style a grey and beige living room with charm and individuality. Remember, it's about pairing the right tones, layering texture, and adding accents that feel like 'you.' Have you ever wondered why some rooms make you feel instantly at ease while others leave you unsettled — even when the furniture is identical? The answer often lies in colour psychology in interior design: the study of how different hues influence our emotions, behaviour, and sense of wellbeing within a space. The colours you choose for your walls, soft furnishings, and artwork are doing far more than decorating — they are quietly shaping how you feel every single day.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Blue is often linked to calmness, but when it comes to Color Psychology, the way you use colours in your space can make a big difference to how you feel every day. I’m excited to share simple ways you can use this powerful tool to create a home that not only looks great but also supports your mood. Be mindful, though, as choosing the wrong shades or combinations could have a negative impact on your space’s atmosphere. Let’s explore how your colour choices can transform your home’s vibe for the better. 

Quick Answer: Colour psychology in interior design is the study of how colours influence mood, emotion, and behaviour in living spaces. Warm colours such as reds and yellows energise a room, while cool tones like blues and greens promote calm. Choosing the right hues for each room helps create a home that supports how you want to feel in it.

Key Takeaways

  • Color helps shape the mood of a room by influencing emotions and behaviour through carefully chosen colours.
  • Warm colours like reds, oranges, and yellows bring energy and warmth, making them ideal for social spaces such as living rooms and kitchens.
  • Cool colours like blues, greens, and purples create calm and serenity, perfect for bedrooms, bathrooms, or relaxing corners.
  • Neutral shades provide balance and can complement bolder colours, giving your space a grounded and sophisticated feel.
  • Using colour theory alongside natural light and room function helps craft interiors that align with your lifestyle and personal style.

1. Understanding Color Psychology

A simple change in colour can transform a room completely, and that’s where Colour Psychology steps in. It’s the study of how colours influence our feelings and behaviours, especially in spaces where we spend so much time, like our homes. I find it fascinating how the shades on your walls or in your furniture can subtly affect your mood, creativity, and even how calm or energised you feel. When used with intention, these colours become powerful tools to create a space that truly reflects your personality while enhancing your wellbeing.

Exploring this concept gives you the chance to make confident decor choices that go beyond mere aesthetics. When you know how different colours speak to the brain and emotions, your home turns into more than just a pretty space. It becomes a personal retreat or a lively hub depending on what vibe you want to create. For anyone invested in interior design, whether you’re a homeowner or an enthusiast, this insight offers endless creative possibilities to make your rooms both beautiful and nurturing.

The Basics of Color Psychology

Colour is everywhere around us, and it directly connects with our senses. Different hues can send various signals to our brain, influencing how we feel and act. For example, blue often feels calming and serene, while red can bring energy and warmth. As you get familiar with the basics of Colour Psychology, you’ll notice that even subtle shifts in shade or intensity can change the mood of a room dramatically.

Most people underestimate how much colours can affect daily life, especially in a home setting. When choosing wall art or textiles, it’s worth thinking about how the colours fit with the atmosphere you want to create. Whether you want to feel more relaxed after a long day or inspired for creativity, the right tones can make a big difference. I always suggest starting simple, testing how certain colours make you feel before committing to a whole room.

How Colour Affects Mood and Emotion

Affects on mood are perhaps the most immediate way colour influences us. For example, yellow often lifts spirits and creates a sense of happiness, while darker colours like deep greys or browns tend to bring a more grounded, comfortable feeling. These emotional responses are why choosing colours for rooms where you want to feel specific emotions matters so much.

Mood plays a huge part in how we experience our living spaces every day. When I help friends or clients pick colours for their walls or artwork, I always remind them that certain colours can either boost positivity or increase stress, depending on how intense or balanced they are. For instance, bright red comes with energy but can feel overwhelming if overused, whereas pastel pink offers softness without too much stimulation. Knowing this helps you combine colours to create harmony and support the atmosphere you want.

For a broader view of how visual choices shape a living space, our guide to art and interior design explores how artwork — not just colour — transforms the mood and identity of a room.

Choosing the Right Colours for Your Space

Assuming you want your home to feel both inviting and inspiring, understanding how to use Color Psychology can transform the way you approach your interior design. The colours you select don’t just add personality; they can influence your mood, energy, and even the way you interact within your space. Whether you’re thinking about calming blues for a bedroom retreat or energising reds for a lively living room, choosing the right colours can help create the atmosphere that best suits your lifestyle and preferences.

When I first started using Color Psychology in my own home, I was amazed at how subtle shifts in tone could make a room feel entirely new. By focusing on colours that reflect your personality and the feeling you want to evoke, you can turn any room into a haven that speaks to both your style and emotional needs. After all, your walls aren’t just backdrops — they can be part of what makes your space feel balanced and peaceful.

2. Factors to Consider When Selecting Colours

You need to think about several key factors when picking colours for your space using Colour Psychology. First, consider the function of the room — a colour that works beautifully in a home office might not be the best choice for a bedroom.

Light levels, room size, and existing furnishings all play a role in how a colour performs. For example, a small, dim room might benefit from lighter, warmer tones to open it up and add warmth.

Next, think about your own emotional response to different colours. Some people find greens calming and refreshing, while others are drawn to the energy of yellows. Your personal taste and how you want to feel in the space matter most. Here are some quick guides to think about:

  • Lighting: Natural and artificial light changes how colours appear.
  • Room Purpose: Relaxing colours for bedrooms, vibrant tones for social spaces.
  • Existing Decor: Make sure colours complement what you already own.
  • Emotional Impact: Choose shades that support your mood or desired atmosphere.

After focusing on these points, you’re better prepared to pick a colour that truly works for your home.

Tips for Creating a Cohesive Colour Palette

There's more to using Color Psychology than simply picking your favourite colour. A cohesive palette helps your interiors feel balanced and connected, avoiding mismatched tones that disrupt the flow of a room. I like to start by choosing a base colour that reflects the overall mood I want, then build around it with complementary or contrasting shades. This gives a room depth and interest without overwhelming the senses.

Here are some simple ways to create a palette that fits your style and space:

  • Start with one main colour and add two or three supporting tones.
  • Use a mix of shades and tints to add variety without clashing.
  • Think about the colour wheel — complementary colours create contrast, while analogous colours bring harmony.
  • Include textures and materials that pick up on your palette to tie everything together.

Any well-thought-out colour palette can effortlessly bring a room together and reflect your personality in a subtle but powerful way.

A personal trick I often use is to gather fabric swatches, paint samples, or even photos that inspire me and arrange them together. This visual approach makes it easier to see how different hues work side by side before committing to a whole room. I also pay close attention to lighting throughout the day, as it can transform how the colours feel. 

  • Gather inspiration from natural elements or travel memories to personalise your palette.
  • Test colours at different times of day to catch shifts in lighting.
  • Choose colours that not only look good but also evoke the mood you desire.
  • Balance bold choices with softer neutral shades.

Any thoughtful approach to Color Psychology will make your space feel uniquely yours and rewarding to spend time in.

3. Applying Color Psychology in Different Rooms

Many of us don’t realise how much the colours in our homes influence our mood and behaviour each day. By using Colour Psychology thoughtfully in different rooms, you can create spaces that feel welcoming, relaxing, or energising — whatever suits your lifestyle best. Whether you want a calming bedroom, a sociable living room, or a refreshing kitchen, the way you use colour can really change the atmosphere. It’s a simple but powerful way to make your home more enjoyable and truly yours.

When applying Colour Psychology, it's helpful to think about the purpose of each room and how you want to feel when you're in it. What suits a lively kitchen might overwhelm a bedroom, and cool tones in the living room could either soothe or feel too cold. I’ve found that understanding the emotional effects behind different shades makes picking wall art and decor so much easier—and more fun!

Living Room

For the living room, which is often the heart of the home, I like to use colours that invite connection and conversation. Warm shades like soft reds, oranges, or golden yellows can create a friendly, welcoming vibe that encourages guests to stay longer. These tones are great if you enjoy lively gatherings or want a space that feels cosy and inviting after a long day.

At the same time, it’s important not to overwhelm the senses with too much intensity. I often suggest mixing warm colours with calming neutrals or cool blues to balance energy and comfort. It’s easy to layer textures and art in complementary colours to keep things interesting without feeling chaotic.

Bedroom

Clearly, the bedroom is all about relaxation and mindfulness, so I lean towards using soft blues, gentle greens, or muted lavenders. These colours are known to lower heart rates and soothe the mind. Using colours here helps create a calm environment that supports better sleep and stress reduction, something many of us value deeply.

Another point I often make is how important lighting is alongside colour in the bedroom. Natural light amplifies the calming effects of cool tones, while softer lamps can add warmth to avoid the room feeling too cold or impersonal. Pairing the right wall art in these colours adds a personal touch that reflects your style and helps set a peaceful mood.

Kitchen

The bedroom might not be the first word you associate with kitchens, but I’ve learned that the colour choices here also directly influence your appetite and energy. For kitchens, I usually recommend vibrant colours like sunny yellows or fresh greens that inspire creativity and help energise your cooking space. These shades can make meal prep feel lively and uplifting, especially during busy mornings.

Room colours in kitchens should be chosen with care since they are often smaller and subject to lots of natural and artificial lighting. Using too much bright red, for example, might cause feelings of restlessness or hunger pangs, so combining intense colour with clean whites or subtle greys often produces the best results.

Bathroom

With bathrooms, I often suggest cooler tones like pale blues or seafoam greens because they promote a sense of cleanliness and calm. These colours can make a small bathroom feel more spacious and spa-like, helping you start or end your day in a refreshing way. Plus, they pair well with natural materials like wood or stone.

Applying colour in your bathroom allows you to create a mini retreat within your home. Adding matching wall art or subtly coloured accessories in these calming hues makes it easier to unwind, making the space feel thoughtfully designed rather than just functional.

4. Combining Colours Effectively

Once again, understanding how colours work is key when you're blending different shades in your space. It’s not just about picking colours you like but how those colours work together to create the mood you want. Combining colours effectively means thinking about how each tone interacts, whether it creates harmony or tension, and how that affects the overall feel of your room.

I’ve found that finding a balance between contrasting and complementary colours often brings a space to life without overwhelming it. When you choose colours carefully, you can guide the mood of any room. For example, pairing vibrant tones with softer hues helps avoid sensory overload while still keeping things lively and inspiring.

Whether you’re repainting a living room or picking out cushions and wall art, considering how each colour influences your vibe is what makes the process rewarding. You’ll start to notice subtle shifts in energy and calmness just by the colour combinations you select.

Understanding Warm vs. Cool Colours

If you’ve ever wondered why some rooms feel cosy while others seem refreshingly calm, warm and cool colours are the answer. Warm colours like reds, oranges, and yellows tend to energise and create a sense of intimacy. I often use these in social spaces or areas where I want to invite conversation and creativity.

On the other hand, cool colours such as blues, greens, and purples bring a tranquil, soothing quality, making them perfect for bedrooms or any spot where you want to unwind.

Knowing the psychology behind warm vs. cool colours helps you decide how to use them to your advantage. From my experience, mixing the two types requires balance so one doesn’t overpower the other—too much warmth can feel overwhelming, while an excess of coolness might feel detached. Pairing a warm accent with a cool background, or vice versa, creates a sense of equilibrium that keeps your space engaging yet comfortable.

Using Neutrals to Balance Bold Colours

Now, let’s talk about how neutrals can be your secret weapon when working with bold colours. If you’re like me and love rich, vibrant tones but worry about them feeling too intense, adding neutrals such as beige, grey, or soft white can tone things down without losing impact. Neutrals act like a calming backdrop, giving your eyes a place to rest and allowing the bold colours to truly stand out.

In my own home, I use neutrals extensively to create a sense of space and airiness, especially with big colour blocks on walls or large furniture pieces. They prevent the room from feeling too busy or chaotic, which is often a risk when working with bright or deep tones. Plus, neutrals offer great flexibility, so you can easily swap your accent colours as your tastes evolve.

Warm neutrals, in particular, bring a welcoming feel that complements bold colours beautifully. Shades like creamy taupe or soft caramel can enrich a room’s atmosphere without stealing attention. They also support sustainable decor choices since these neutral bases tend to pair well with natural materials, creating a calming, grounded environment that speaks to both your sense of style and mindfulness.

Using Artwork to Enhance Your Colour Choices

Not all colours in a room need to come from paint or furnishings. Artwork offers a fantastic way to bring your favourite hues into a space and tie everything together. When you use Color Psychology thoughtfully, artwork can boost the mood you want for your room, whether it’s calm, uplifting, or energising.

I’ve found that carefully chosen pieces add depth and personality to any interior, making the atmosphere feel more welcoming and balanced. Artwork doesn’t just fill space; it interacts with your existing palette, playing off walls and textiles to enhance how colours feel in your environment.

Selecting Art That Complements Your Palette

Any successful design starts with knowing which colours you want to highlight in your home. When picking out art, I suggest choosing pieces that share tones with your room or bring in contrasting shades that still work harmoniously. For example, if your palette leans towards cool blues and greys, a burst of warm oranges or yellows in art can create an energising balance, while keeping everything in tune with the principles of Color and Psychology.

Think about the mood each colour in your artwork provokes and how it relates to the room’s purpose. A bedroom designed for calming rest benefits from art in soft greens or blues, whereas a lively dining room can benefit from brighter red or gold accents. Trusting your instincts on what feels right while keeping the psychological aspects of colour in mind helps to choose art that truly complements your existing palette.

5. Tips for Displaying Art 

Choices in how you display your artwork can change the way Colors affects your space. Lighting, positioning, and grouping all influence how colours come across and impact mood. I always recommend positioning pieces where natural or soft artificial light highlights the artwork without causing glare or harsh shadows. It’s also worth considering the eye level and grouping art so that colour flows naturally around the room.

  • Use warm lights to enhance reds, yellows, and oranges for a cosier feeling.
  • Neutral or cool white lighting helps blues and greens keep their calming effect.
  • Group artworks with complementary colours close together to create colour harmony.
  • Leave enough space around each piece to avoid overwhelming the senses.

Knowing how you display your artwork allows you to make the most of its Color potential, creating an environment that genuinely supports your mood and lifestyle.

Seasonal Colour Changes

Despite the fact that our homes often stay the same all year round, Color Psychology shows how bringing in seasonal colour changes can greatly influence the mood and energy in a room. I find that tweaking your palette according to the seasons not only keeps your space feeling fresh but also helps you connect with the natural rhythms outside your window.

For example, warm tones like burnt orange and deep reds can add a cosy, inviting atmosphere during the cooler months, while brighter shades like soft yellows and light blues work wonders in spring and summer to lift your spirits.

Changing colours throughout the year taps into how we naturally respond to different environments, which is at the heart of Color in interior design. When you adapt your home to seasonal shifts, you create a dynamic space that supports your well-being. I love how simple swaps in cushions, throws, or wall art can transform a room’s vibe without a full redesign. Seasonal updates like these can make your space feel more aligned with your lifestyle and the world outside.

Refreshing Your Space with Seasonal Colours

Any change in season offers a perfect excuse to refresh your space through colour. It’s amazing how adding just a few seasonal hues can breathe new life into your rooms. From soft pastels to rich jewel tones, these subtle shifts can support how you feel throughout the year. For instance, calming greens and blues in spring help create an uplifting, peaceful atmosphere, which is ideal for areas where you want to relax or work.

I’ve noticed that working with seasonal colours feels like a natural way to reset your environment without overwhelming your style. Whether it’s swapping curtains, changing up wall art, or layering in new cushions, you’re tapping into the power of Color to make your home a soothing and inspiring place all year. It feels more like a journey than a chore, as if your home evolves with you.

Tips for Transitional Decor

An easy way to handle seasonal colour changes is by using transitional decor. This approach blends the current season’s palette with the upcoming one, giving your space a smoother shift without feeling jarring. For example, when moving from summer to autumn, try introducing amber tones alongside the lighter summery shades you already love.

Transitional decor uses layering to create interest and depth while honouring the psychology of colour to enhance comfort and mood.

Here are some tips I find helpful for creating transitional decor:

  • Choose Color-informed hues that work well together, like warm neutrals with subtle pops of the new season’s bright shades.
  • Use accessories like throws, rugs, and cushions to introduce fresh colours without major changes.
  • Incorporate natural elements, such as plants or wooden accents, that complement both seasonal palettes.

Perceiving your home as a living space that moves with the seasons can make decorating feel more intuitive and enjoyable.

Final Words 

Summing up, using Color in interior design is a wonderful way to shape how your home feels and functions. When I think about the colours I bring into a room, I focus on how they make me and others feel—whether it's calm, energised, or inspired. By applying some simple ideas about colour, you can create spaces that truly reflect your personality and support your daily mood and lifestyle.

More about

If you want to learn more about how different colours can influence your home, I highly recommend checking out The Psychology of Colours in Interior Design. It’s a great resource that helped me better understand the impact of colour choices and gave me fresh ideas for my own spaces. I’m sure you’ll find plenty of inspiration there to help you make confident colour decisions and transform your living areas beautifully.

Getting familiar with interior decorating terms like hue, tone, and saturation will make it much easier to apply colour psychology effectively in your own home.

Avoid heavy, dark colours alongside grey as they tend to shrink the perception of space. Instead, pair your grey with these lighter tones on walls, furniture, or accessories. Reflective surfaces like mirrors or glossy furniture finishes also complement the effect.

Test your chosen colours with patches on the walls to see them at different times of day, ensuring they suit your sleeping space perfectly.

An accent wall can completely change how a room feels — but what actually makes one work? It's not just about picking a bold colour or hanging a single print; the real difference comes from understanding scale, placement, and how art interacts with the space around it. Get those fundamentals right, and even the most understated wall becomes the visual heart of the room.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Quick Answer: An accent wall is a single wall treated differently from the others — through colour, texture, wallpaper, or art — to create a focal point in a room. The most effective feature walls combine the right wall choice (usually the one your eye naturally travels to) with art or colour that complements the rest of the space. Done well, a feature wall can make a room feel larger, more cohesive, and far more considered.

Have you ever thought about how a well-styled feature wall can give any room an instant upgrade?

The right wall art paired with a feature wall doesn’t just decorate—it completely transforms how your space feels.

Many people assume bold colours or trendy patterns are all it takes, but studies show that a strategically placed accent wall can actually make a room feel up to 30 percent larger and far more stylish than traditional decorating methods.

Surprising, isn’t it? The real magic happens when you choose and style your wall art thoughtfully—get this part right, and even the dullest corner can take on a personality of its own.

If you want to take your display further, our guide to creating a calm living room art wall walks through colour palettes, print selection, and layout ideas in detail.

1: Choose the Right Wall

Not every wall is created equal, and knowing how to identify the ideal canvas can make a significant difference in your home's overall aesthetic.

When planning your feature wall, focus on walls that naturally draw the eye and complement your room's existing architecture. According to DIY Doctor, strategic wall selection is crucial for creating visual impact.

Key considerations for choosing your accent wall include:

  • Structural prominence: Select walls without interruptions like windows or doors
  • Room orientation: Choose walls that create natural visual balance
  • Existing architectural features: Chimney breasts or alcoves can serve as excellent accent wall locations

Not all rooms are identical, so you’ll want to evaluate your specific space carefully. In living rooms, the wall behind the sofa or facing the entrance often works brilliantly. Bedrooms might benefit from the wall behind the headboard, while dining areas could highlight walls near key furniture pieces.

Consider the room’s natural light and traffic flow when making your selection. A wall that receives ample natural light can help your art piece shine, while avoiding high-traffic areas prevents potential damage.

Pro tip: Use painter’s tape to temporarily mark potential accent walls. This allows you to visualise the potential impact before making a permanent commitment. Step back, observe from different angles, and imagine how your chosen wall art types will transform the space.

Remember, the right wall acts as a storytelling backdrop for your art, creating a focal point that captures attention and reflects your personal style.

2: Consider Your Colour Scheme

The colour scheme you select plays a pivotal role in transforming your accent wall art from a mere decoration to a powerful design statement. Colour is not just visual; it communicates emotion, sets mood, and creates atmosphere within your living space.

According to National Design Academy, colour can fundamentally alter room perception before any furniture is positioned. Your chosen palette will serve as the foundational backdrop for your wall art, making it crucial to select harmonious tones.

Consider these essential colour scheme strategies:

  • Complementary colours: Select art that either matches or intentionally contrasts with your wall colour
  • Mood setting: Choose colours that reflect the emotional tone you want in the room
  • Existing decor: Ensure your wall art integrates seamlessly with current furniture and design elements

Neutral walls provide incredible versatility, allowing bold art pieces to become striking focal points. Soft greys, warm whites, and muted beiges create elegant canvases that let artwork truly shine. Conversely, deep, rich wall colours like navy, emerald, or burgundy can create dramatic backdrops that make art feel more intense and sophisticated.

Psychological colour principles matter immensely. Warm tones like terracotta and mustard can create intimate, energetic spaces, while cool blues and greens promote calmness and tranquillity. Your wall colour should complement your art’s emotional narrative.

When selecting your colour scheme, consider lighting conditions. Natural and artificial light dramatically impact how colours appear throughout the day. Test paint samples at different times to understand their true character.

Pro tip: Use interior decor ideas to experiment with colour combinations before committing. Digital design tools and sample swatches can help visualise potential arrangements, ensuring your accent wall art creates the exact atmosphere you desire.

3: Use Large-Scale Artwork

Large-scale artwork represents the ultimate statement piece in accent wall design, transforming ordinary spaces into extraordinary visual experiences. These expansive art pieces do more than decorate - they redefine the entire atmosphere of a room.

According to the National Design Academy, large-scale artwork serves as a powerful focal point, providing colour, texture, and a sense of completeness to interior spaces.

Key advantages of incorporating large-scale artwork include:

  • Dramatic visual impact: Creates an immediate, compelling focal point
  • Space perception: Can make rooms feel larger and more intentionally designed
  • Emotional resonance: Allows for deeper artistic expression and connection

Proportions matter significantly when selecting large-scale art. A piece should typically occupy approximately two-thirds to three-quarters of your accent wall’s width. This creates visual balance without overwhelming the space. Consider oversized photographic prints, abstract canvases, or expansive mixed-media installations that command attention.

SHOP HERE

Texture becomes crucial with large artworks. Dimensional pieces like sculptural wall hangings or textured canvas prints add depth and intrigue. These three-dimensional elements catch light differently throughout the day, creating dynamic visual experiences.

When selecting your large-scale artwork, consider your room’s existing architecture and furniture. The art should complement, not compete with, other design elements. Minimalist spaces benefit from bold, graphic pieces, while more ornate rooms might require more subdued, textural artwork.

Pro tip: Before purchasing, use painter’s tape to mark the potential artwork’s dimensions on your wall. This visual representation helps you understand scale and placement. If you need inspiration for solving focal point challenges, this technique can be incredibly helpful.

Remember, large-scale artwork is an investment in your home’s aesthetic narrative - choose pieces that speak to you and reflect your personal style.

4: Create a Gallery Wall

A gallery wall represents an extraordinary opportunity to transform your accent wall into a personalised narrative of art, memories, and visual storytelling. This approach allows you to curate a dynamic and deeply personal display that goes far beyond traditional single-piece artwork.

According to the UK government’s research on art and design, engaging with art enables individuals to explore creativity and express personal imagination.

Essential considerations for crafting a compelling gallery wall include:

  • Visual cohesion: Select pieces with complementary colour palettes or themes
  • Varied frame styles: Mix different frame sizes, materials, and textures
  • Personal significance: Include artwork that tells your unique story

Composition is key when designing your gallery wall. Start by laying out your selected pieces on the floor, experimenting with arrangements before committing to wall placement. This technique allows you to visualise the overall composition and make adjustments without unnecessary wall damage.

SHOP HERE

Consider creating a balanced yet intentionally asymmetrical layout. 

Artwork positioning should feel organic - avoid strict grid formations. Mix larger statement pieces with smaller complementary frames to create visual interest and depth. Maintain consistent spacing between pieces, typically 5-10 centimetres, to create a unified look.

Diversity in artwork style can elevate your gallery wall from mundane to magnificent. Combine different mediums like photographs, watercolour prints, sketches, and even three-dimensional objects. This eclectic approach ensures your wall feels curated rather than cluttered.

If you’re unsure how to hang art in challenging spaces, our guide on hanging wall art can provide additional techniques for unique wall configurations.

Remember, a gallery wall is a living, evolving display. Don’t be afraid to rotate pieces, add new artwork, or adjust your arrangement as your tastes and life experiences change.

5: Incorporate Textured Elements

Texture transforms accent wall art from two-dimensional decoration to a multisensory experience that engages not just sight, but touch and perception. Textural elements create depth, intrigue, and visual complexity that elevate your wall art from ordinary to extraordinary.

According to the National Design Academy, incorporating natural materials can create a warm, calming environment that resonates with our innate connection to organic surfaces.

Consider these textural techniques for your accent wall:

  • Dimensional wall hangings: Macramé, woven tapestries, and sculptural pieces
  • Mixed media artwork: Combine painting, fabric, and three-dimensional objects
  • Relief techniques: Incorporate raised elements like wood carving or embossed metals

Natural materials offer exceptional textural opportunities. Wooden panels, rattan installations, and woven textile art pieces introduce organic warmth and tactile richness. Think beyond traditional flat artwork - explore three-dimensional wall sculptures that cast interesting shadows and create visual movement.

Metal artwork provides another sophisticated textural option. Copper, brass, and steel pieces can introduce metallic textures that reflect light differently throughout the day. Hammered, brushed, or patinated metal surfaces add complexity and intrigue to your accent wall.

Consider layering textures for maximum impact. A ceramic wall installation paired with a wooden frame, or a textile piece mounted on a sleek metal background, creates visual dialogue and depth. The interplay between different materials tells a richer story than a single, uniform surface.

If your space feels monotonous, explore techniques for breaking neutral tones by introducing varied textures. This approach prevents visual flatness and adds dynamic interest.

Remember, texture is about creating an emotional connection. Choose pieces that not only look compelling but also invite touch and contemplation.

6: Mix Artistic Styles

Mixing artistic styles transforms your accent wall from a simple display into a sophisticated narrative of visual diversity. Eclectic combinations breathe life and personality into your living spaces, creating a unique artistic landscape that reflects your individual aesthetic journey.

According to the University of the Arts London, understanding and reinterpreting classic styles can dramatically inform contemporary interior design approaches.

Key principles for successfully blending artistic styles include:

  • Colour harmony: Select pieces with complementary colour palettes
  • Scale balance: Mix larger statement pieces with smaller, intricate artworks
  • Thematic connection: Find subtle visual or emotional threads between different styles

Contemporary art can beautifully coexist with traditional pieces when approached thoughtfully. A minimalist geometric print might sit elegantly beside a vintage botanical illustration, creating a dialogue between different artistic eras and sensibilities. The secret lies in finding unexpected yet harmonious connections.

Consider juxtaposing contrasting artistic movements. A sleek, abstract digital print could create fascinating tension when placed near a classic watercolour landscape. These deliberate style contrasts generate visual intrigue and prevent your accent wall from feeling monotonous.

Texture and framing play crucial roles in style mixing. Uniform frames can help unify diverse artworks, while varied frame styles can emphasise the intentional eclecticism of your display. Metallic frames, wooden frames, and minimalist white frames can each contribute to your artistic narrative.

If you’re struggling to add personality to your space, explore strategies for enhancing room decor that go beyond traditional styling approaches.

Remember, artistic style mixing is about creating a personal museum wall that tells your unique story - embrace imperfection and let your creativity guide you.

7: Personalise Your Feature Wall with Meaningful Art

DIY art represents the most intimate and meaningful approach to creating an accent wall, transforming your space into a deeply personal canvas that tells your unique story. Handcrafted artwork becomes an extension of your own creativity, reflecting memories, emotions, and individual experiences.

According to the Museum of the Home, personal expression through art is a powerful way to make living spaces feel truly yours.

Consider these DIY art techniques for your accent wall:

  • Photography projects: Create personalised photo collages or printed memories
  • Mixed media artwork: Combine painting, fabric, and found objects
  • Craft-based installations: Experiment with macramé, paper art, or textile designs

Affordable materials can yield stunning results. Watercolour papers, canvas boards, and acrylic paints provide accessible entry points for artistic experimentation. You don’t need professional training - just enthusiasm and willingness to explore.

Photographic memories offer exceptional DIY potential. Transform personal travel photographs, family portraits, or meaningful landscape shots into large-scale art pieces. Black and white prints or sepia-toned images can add sophisticated elegance to your accent wall.

Textile arts like embroidery, weaving, or fabric painting introduce textural dimension. A hand-stitched wall hanging or a painted fabric panel can become a captivating focal point that tells a deeply personal narrative.

  1. Creating Contrast with Greige: Incorporating Bold Colours and Patterns

Greige is a neutral base for incorporating bold colours and patterns. Add vibrancy with patterned throw pillows or statement furniture pieces against a greige backdrop for a balanced look. 

  1. Greige Exteriors: Applying the Timeless Blend to Outdoor Spaces

Extend greige colours to your home's exterior with paint choices for siding, trim, and accents. Enhance curb appeal by integrating greige landscaping elements and outdoor decor. 

Keeping Greige Surfaces and Fabrics Clean and Fresh

Proper cleaning techniques suited to different materials are needed to maintain greige surfaces and fabrics. Regular upkeep ensures that greige paint, upholstery, and other surfaces remain pristine over time. 

Embracing Greige as a Timeless and Versatile Design Choice

Greige colours offer a timeless and versatile foundation for home decor, fostering balance and harmony while allowing for personalisation and creativity. Whether used on walls, furniture, or accessories, greige creates a sophisticated atmosphere that adapts to various design preferences and trends. Incorporate greige into your home decor to achieve a cohesive, inviting space that stands the test of time.

What makes greige wall art work in any room?

The reason greige tones translate so well to unique wall art is the same reason they work on walls and furniture: they carry both warmth and restraint in equal measure. A print in sandy taupe, warm stone, or dusty putty reads as sophisticated without dominating the room — it anchors the space without competing with soft furnishings or architectural features.

Abstract pieces with layered neutral washes are the most versatile choice, as they echo the natural depth of greige paint colours. Nature-inspired prints — think botanical line drawings, misty landscape photography, or textured sand dune imagery — also sit beautifully within a greige-led scheme because they draw from the same earthy, organic palette.

Minimalist compositions in warm off-white and charcoal are another strong option: they introduce contrast without breaking the calm, cohesive feel that makes greige interiors so appealing. The key is to choose artwork whose background or dominant tone shares that grey-beige midpoint, rather than pulling sharply warm or sharply cool.

How to style greige art prints: room-by-room guide

Living room: A set of three matching prints in warm stone and charcoal tones works well above a greige sofa or flanking a fireplace. Gallery walls in mixed frames — brushed brass, natural oak, and matte black — add visual interest while keeping the palette cohesive.

Bedroom: Large-format botanical or abstract prints in taupe and cream tones create a restful focal point above the bed. Stick to two or three pieces rather than a busy gallery to preserve the calm, sanctuary feel.

Hallway: A single oversized landscape print in warm sandy neutrals makes a confident first impression. Opt for horizontal formats to elongate the space and draw the eye through the room.

Home office: Architectural line drawings or minimalist typography prints in greige tones add personality without distraction — ideal for a space where focus matters as much as style.

Greige vs taupe vs beige: which is right for your artwork?

These three neutral tones are often used interchangeably, but understanding the difference helps you choose artwork that genuinely complements your scheme rather than clashing with it.

Greige sits squarely between grey and beige — it has a cooler edge than beige but more warmth than a mid grey. It suits contemporary and Scandi-influenced interiors particularly well.

Taupe leans slightly darker and browner, with more of a clay or mushroom quality. It works beautifully alongside deep wood tones and leather, and suits transitional or country-cottage schemes.

Beige is the warmest of the three, with golden or sandy undertones. It pairs naturally with cream, terracotta, and natural linen — ideal for relaxed, biophilic, or French-country interiors.

When choosing prints, hold a paint chip or fabric swatch next to the artwork if possible — or check whether the product image is photographed on a warm or cool background, as this gives a reliable indication of how it will read in your room.

Whether you're furnishing a studio flat or a one-bedroom apartment, smart wall decor choices make a disproportionately big impact on how spacious and cohesive your home feels.

Have you ever felt overwhelmed trying to make a studio apartment feel spacious, functional, and stylish all at once? Living in a small space doesn't mean sacrificing comfort or design. With the right studio apartment ideas, you can transform even the tiniest space into a well-organized, beautiful home that works for your lifestyle.

Quick Answer: The best wall decor ideas for small apartments use vertical space, light-reflecting mirrors, and carefully scaled artwork to make rooms feel larger. A single oversized print, a curated two or three-piece set, or a compact gallery wall adds personality without cluttering the floor. Stick to a cohesive colour palette and hang pieces at eye level to keep the space feeling open and intentional.

In my experience helping people maximize their small spaces, I've seen how smart design solutions—from multifunctional furniture to clever zoning—can completely change how a studio apartment feels. The key is making every square metre count whilst maintaining a sense of openness and calm.

Defining Zones in Your Studio Apartment

Creating distinct zones in a studio apartment helps it feel more organized and functional. Use furniture placement, rugs, or room dividers to separate sleeping, living, and working areas.

Visual Separation

A bookshelf, folding screen, or even a strategically placed sofa can create boundaries between zones without blocking light or making the space feel cramped.

Multifunctional Furniture Solutions

Multifunctional furniture is essential in studio apartments. Every piece should serve more than one purpose to maximize your limited space.

Smart Furniture Choices

  • Sofa beds for sleeping and seating
  • Storage ottomans that double as coffee tables
  • Wall-mounted fold-down desks
  • Beds with built-in storage drawers
  • Nesting tables that tuck away when not needed

Maximizing Vertical Storage

When floor space is limited, think vertically. Floor-to-ceiling shelving, wall-mounted storage, and hanging organizers make the most of your walls.

Vertical Solutions

Install floating shelves above doorways, use tall bookcases, and hang hooks for bags and coats. This keeps floors clear and makes the space feel larger.

Light and Colour to Expand Space
